title: Levels of Biological Organisation
seo_title: JSS 1 Intermediate Science: Levels of Biological Organisation Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: JSS 1 Intermediate Science: Living and Non-Living Things
standard_text: Living things are organised from cells to tissues, organs, organ systems and organisms; specialised cells form tissues with special functions. (summary of the Intermediate Science curriculum, JSS 1, theme: Living and Non-Living Things)
meta_desc: Free JSS 1 Intermediate Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Living and Non-Living Things): specialised cells and tissues, organs and organ systems, the digestive and respiratory systems, the circulatory system and plant tissues and organs. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
key_sub: Organ systems work together to keep the body alive.
body_html:
How to think about it

Cells with the same job form a tissue. Animals have four tissue types: epithelial (covers), connective (supports, such as bone and blood), muscle (moves) and nerve (signals). Tissues form organs such as the stomach, and organs work together in systems.

The digestive system breaks food down and absorbs nutrients; the respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide; the circulatory system carries them around the body. Plants have dermal, ground and vascular tissue; their organs are roots, stems, leaves and flowers, organised into the root system and the shoot system.

Example

Put in order: organ, cell, organ system, tissue.

Smallest first

Answer: cell, tissue, organ, organ system

Example

Which two systems work together to get oxygen to the muscles?

One takes in oxygen, one carries it.

Answer: respiratory and circulatory

Common mistakes

  • Calling blood an organ: it is a connective tissue.
  • Thinking organ systems work alone.
  • Saying plants have no tissues.

faq.q: Why are red blood cells specialised?
faq.a: They have no nucleus and are full of haemoglobin, so they carry as much oxygen as possible.
It carries water and minerals from the roots to the leaves.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a xylem vessel?
c: no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls
items.e: A xylem vessel has no cytoplasm or cross-walls and lignified walls: an empty, continuous tube that carries water and gives support.

items.q: How does a frog breathe in water?
c: it does not breathe in water
items.e: On land it also uses its lungs and buccal cavity.

items.q: At which level of organisation is the shoot system of a plant?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which cell has a thicker inner wall, giving a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma?
items.e: Each specialised cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: At which level of organisation is the stomach?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: At which level of organisation is the circulatory system?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a sperm cell?
c: no nucleus and a biconcave shape
items.e: A sperm cell has a tail (flagellum) and many mitochondria: energy to swim to the egg.

items.q: What is the main nitrogenous waste of a frog?
items.e: Tadpoles excrete ammonia.

items.q: A palisade mesophyll cell has many chloroplasts. How does this help it?
c: a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts
energy to swim to the egg
a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: At which level of organisation is xylem tissue?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which tissue matches this description: the wall of the stomach and intestine?
items.e: Smooth muscle: the wall of the stomach and intestine.

items.q: Which cell has a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body, giving many proteins made and packaged for secretion?
c: a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes
items.e: Each specialised cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: Which cell has a long, narrow extension, giving a larger surface area to absorb water and mineral salts?
c: a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes
items.e: Each specialised cell is adapted to its job.

items.q: What does a male frog have that a female does not?
c: vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of the forelimb
items.e: These help the male call and hold the female.

items.q: Where is ligament found, or what does it do?
c: just beneath the skin, as a support framework
connecting a bone to another bone
the lining of the stomach and intestine, with tall cells
the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs
items.e: Ligament: connecting a bone to another bone.

items.q: At which level of organisation is the heart?
items.e: cell → tissue (similar cells) → organ (several tissues) → organ system → organism.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a guard cell?
c: a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body
items.e: A guard cell has a thicker inner wall: a change of shape that opens and closes the stoma.

items.q: Which tissue matches this description: the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs?
items.e: Squamous epithelium: the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs.

items.q: Where is columnar epithelium found, or what does it do?
c: the lining of the stomach and intestine, with tall cells
the wall of the stomach and intestine
connecting a bone to another bone
items.e: Columnar epithelium: the lining of the stomach and intestine, with tall cells.

items.q: Which feature is typical of a pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes?
c: no nucleus and a biconcave shape
a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body
items.e: A pancreatic cell that secretes enzymes has a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi body: many proteins made and packaged for secretion.

items.q: Which organ system does the brain belong to?
items.e: The brain is part of the nervous system.

items.q: Nonso reads about a body system that supports the body and protects organs. Which system is it?
items.e: The skeletal system supports the body and protects organs.

items.q: Which organ system does the skin belong to?
items.e: The skin is part of the integumentary system.

items.q: Which organ system does the stomach belong to?
items.e: The stomach is part of the digestive system.

items.q: What level is made of many cells working together?
items.e: Many cells make up a tissue.

items.q: Which organ system does the pancreas (making insulin) belong to?
items.e: The pancreas (making insulin) is part of the endocrine system.

items.q: Tobi asks: what is the main job of the respiratory system?
c: It supports the body and protects organs.
It moves the body by pulling on bones.
It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
It takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
items.e: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for removing wastes from the blood?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which organ system does the white blood cells belong to?
items.e: The white blood cells is part of the immune system.

items.q: What level comes right after tissue (going from small to large)?
items.e: tissue → organ.

items.q: Which level is the largest?
items.e: An organism is made of all its systems.

items.q: Chioma reads about a body system that removes wastes from the body. Which system is it?
items.e: The excretory system removes wastes from the body.

items.q: Which list goes from smallest to largest?
c: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
cell → tissue → organ system → organ → organism
tissue → cell → organ → organ system → organism
items.e: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.

items.q: Which level of organisation is bone tissue?
items.e: Bone tissue is a tissue.

items.q: Obinna reads about a body system that takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide. Which system is it?
items.e: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: What level comes right after organ system (going from small to large)?
items.e: organ system → organism.

items.q: Which organ system does the lungs belong to?
items.e: The lungs is part of the respiratory system.

items.q: Chiamaka asks: what is the main job of the excretory system?
c: It removes wastes from the body.
It supports the body and protects organs.
It takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
items.e: The excretory system removes wastes from the body.

items.q: Which organ system does the diaphragm belong to?
items.e: The diaphragm is part of the respiratory system.

items.q: Kelechi asks: what is the main job of the circulatory system?
c: It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It supports the body and protects organs.
It takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
items.e: The circulatory system moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It makes pancreatic juice with carbohydrase, protease and lipase.
items.e: The pancreas: It makes pancreatic juice with carbohydrase, protease and lipase.

items.q: Teeth chew a piece of bread into small pieces. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: Protease in the stomach breaks proteins into smaller pieces. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: Carbohydrase from the pancreas breaks starch into sugars. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: What is the main job of the rectum?
c: It absorbs water and mineral salts from undigested food.
It completes digestion and absorbs digested food into the blood.
It moves food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis.
It stores faeces before they are removed from the body.
items.e: The rectum: It stores faeces before they are removed from the body.

items.q: What is the job of the bronchi?
c: A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through the trachea (windpipe). Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches the trachea (windpipe)?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: What is the job of the trachea (windpipe)?
c: Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through a bronchiole. Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: What is the job of the ribs?
c: Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Bones that protect the lungs and heart.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system does this? It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.
items.e: The stomach: It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.

items.q: What is the main job of the gall bladder?
c: It churns food and makes gastric juice with protease and acid to start digesting proteins.
It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.
It makes bile, which breaks fats into small droplets.
It completes digestion and absorbs digested food into the blood.
items.e: The gall bladder: It stores bile until it is needed in the small intestine.

items.q: What is the job of the bronchioles?
c: Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: The tongue rolls chewed food into a ball. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: What does protease break proteins down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: What is the job of cilia?
c: Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.
Muscles between the ribs that move the ribcage up and out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: The incisors bite off a piece of an apple. Is this physical or chemical digestion?
items.e: Physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces; chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large molecules into small ones.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Blood enters the left ventricle. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the aorta to the kidney?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A student counts 18 pulse beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 18 × (60 ÷ 15).

items.q: A student counts 14 pulse beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate in beats per minute?
items.e: Heart rate = 14 × (60 ÷ 15).

items.q: Does the pulmonary vein carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

items.q: Blood is in the vena cava. Where does it go next?
items.e: Body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood back to the heart?
items.e: A vein carries blood back to the heart.

items.q: Does the pulmonary artery carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 72 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 75 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 72 × 75 = 5,400 cm³/min.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells?
items.e: A capillary carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood to the muscle of the heart wall?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 65 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 80 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 65 × 80 = 5,200 cm³/min.

items.q: What does an artery do?
c: It carries blood back to the heart.
It carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.
It carries blood away from the heart.
items.e: An artery carries blood away from the heart.

items.q: A person has a heart rate of 120 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 90 cm³. What is the cardiac output in dm³ per minute?
items.e: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume = 120 × 90 = 10,800 cm³/min.

items.q: Does the aorta carry oxygenated or deoxygenated blood?
items.e: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the body to the right atrium?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the left ventricle to the body?
items.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back.

items.q: Which blood vessel has a wall only one cell thick?
items.e: A capillary has a wall only one cell thick.

items.q: Blood enters the left atrium. Where has it just come from?
items.e: Follow the double circulation backwards.

items.q: Which tissue transports amino acids in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Sugars move from the leaves to the growing shoot tip. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Mineral salts absorbed by the roots reach the leaves. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts. How does this help the leaf?
c: They open and close the stoma to control water loss.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: A rose in blue-coloured water develops blue streaks in its petals. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Sugar made in the leaves is carried to the fruits of a mango tree. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Leaves have veins (xylem and phloem). How does this help the leaf?
c: They have a large surface area to absorb light.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Which tissue transports sucrose in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: What is sapwood?
c: the light-coloured outer wood that still conducts water
items.e: Also called alburnum.

items.q: Which description fits palisade parenchyma?
c: tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis
specialised parenchyma cells linked to sieve tubes
living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
items.e: Palisade parenchyma: tall, closely packed cells with many chloroplasts below the upper epidermis.

items.q: Palisade cells are near the top of the leaf. How does this help the leaf?
c: Gases can move easily between the cells.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
They have a large surface area to absorb light.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Which description fits bulliform cells?
c: living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
a waxy layer on the epidermis that cuts water loss
specialised parenchyma cells linked to sieve tubes
large empty cells in grass leaves that make them roll up in dry weather
items.e: Bulliform cells: large empty cells in grass leaves that make them roll up in dry weather.

items.q: Which elements of xylem are found mainly in angiosperms?
items.e: Gymnosperms lack vessels.

items.q: A ring of bark is removed from a tree and the bark above the ring swells with sugar. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Food made in the leaves is stored in the tubers of a tapioca plant. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Which description fits medullary rays?
c: dead cells with thick lignified walls that give mechanical support
living cells thickened at the corners with cellulose and pectin
parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem
the layers just below the epidermis, of collenchyma in dicot stems
items.e: Medullary rays: parenchyma cells between the vascular bundles of a dicot stem.

items.q: The lower surface has many stomata. How does this help the leaf?
c: Carbon dioxide can diffuse in and oxygen can diffuse out.
They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.

items.q: Which tissue transports water and mineral ions in a flowering plant?
items.e: Xylem: water and mineral ions, upwards. Phloem: sucrose and amino acids (translocation), up and down.

items.q: Water moves up from the roots to the leaves of a balsam plant. Which tissue is involved?
items.e: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves; phloem transports food (sugars) made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.q: Leaves are thin. How does this help the leaf?
c: They can absorb lots of light for photosynthesis.
They bring water and carry away sugars.
Carbon dioxide only has a short distance to diffuse to the cells.
items.e: Leaf structure fits its job.
